title: Meta Just Paid $900 Million for an Indian Fintech. Its Founder Will Now Run WhatsApp.
excerpt: Kunal Shah built CRED from $1 million of his own money into a $4.5 billion company. Now he's taking over the world's biggest messaging platform — and Meta's biggest bet on payments.
body:
When Kunal Shah posted a brief message on social media on Monday, it carried the weight of two announcements that would have been blockbusters on their own. Together, they mark the single largest bet a Western tech giant has ever placed on an Indian founder.

Meta Platforms, the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, will invest $900 million in CRED — the Bengaluru-based fintech that rewards users for paying credit card bills — valuing the company at roughly $4.5 billion. As part of the deal, Shah, who founded CRED with $1 million of his own capital in 2018, will step away from day-to-day operations and take charge of WhatsApp globally.

"CRED is ready for its next phase. I am stepping back," Shah said. "As for me, I'll be joining Meta to lead WhatsApp globally."

The dual transaction — investment and leadership transition — was structured simultaneously, with six major existing investors including Peak XV Partners, Tiger Global and GIC selling stakes to Meta. Miten Sampat, who has led strategy and finance at CRED since 2020, will step in as interim CEO.

## Why Meta Wants an Indian Fintech Builder

The appointment is not a ceremonial hire. WhatsApp has more than two billion users globally, with India alone accounting for over 500 million of them — making it the platform's largest market. But despite years of trying, WhatsApp Pay has barely dented India's digital payments market, where PhonePe and Google Pay together control over 85 per cent of transactions processed through the Unified Payments Interface.

Meta's chief product officer, Chris Cox, wrote in an internal memo that the company had been looking for a leader with "an intuitive grasp of the immense, global product potential for WhatsApp." Shah, who built FreeCharge into one of India's leading digital payments platforms before selling it and then built CRED into a company processing billions in transactions, fit the profile.

"Kunal built CRED into one of India's most important technology companies, and he brings the kind of builder mentality and global perspective that will serve him well in running the world's biggest messaging app," Mark Zuckerberg said in a statement.

Industry executives say the move signals Meta's ambitions to turn WhatsApp into a "superapp" — a platform that handles messaging, payments, commerce and financial services in a single interface. The model has worked spectacularly in Asia, with WeChat in China processing trillions of dollars in transactions annually. WhatsApp, despite its reach, has never cracked that code.

## The CRED Story: From Nothing to $4.5 Billion

Shah's journey is the kind that animates startup mythology but also grounds it in reality. After selling FreeCharge to Axis Bank in 2017, he spent nearly three years investing and experimenting before launching CRED in 2018 with a simple idea: reward people who pay their credit card bills on time.

The concept drew scepticism. India's credit card user base was small — roughly 35 million cards at the time — and the revenue model was unclear. But CRED grew to 17 million members by 2025, launched products spanning payments, lending, insurance, commerce and wealth management, and scaled annual revenue to approximately $325 million. The company recorded its first profitable quarter this year.

The $900 million from Meta includes both primary investment — new capital flowing into CRED — and secondary purchases of shares from existing shareholders. The deal also includes $100 million in Meta advertising credits, according to reports. Shah will retain a roughly 20 per cent stake in CRED while stepping back from an executive role. Meta will hold approximately 20 per cent but will not take a board seat.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

The deal sends multiple signals. For Indian entrepreneurs, it validates the idea that a founder can build a company in India, scale it to global relevance, and then be recruited to lead one of the world's most important platforms. Shah, 47, has no engineering degree and no Silicon Valley pedigree — his career was built entirely in India's digital payments ecosystem.

For the 500 million Indians who use WhatsApp daily, the appointment raises questions about what comes next. If Shah succeeds in making WhatsApp a credible payments and commerce platform in India, it could reshape how hundreds of millions of people manage their money. India's central bank and regulators are likely to watch closely — calls to review the deal on competition grounds have already surfaced.

CRED itself faces a transition. With its founder gone and an IPO on the horizon, the company will need to prove it can sustain growth without its most visible champion. Five ESOP buybacks — including one announced alongside this deal — have built goodwill among employees. But the test now is execution under new leadership.

For Meta, the $900 million is a calculated risk. The company has struggled to monetise WhatsApp despite its massive user base. Shah's appointment is an acknowledgement that cracking payments in emerging markets requires not just technology but the kind of lived understanding of consumer behaviour that only comes from building in those markets. The delta between WhatsApp's current reality and its potential, as Shah himself put it, remains massive.

"While it's come very far," he said, "the delta between WhatsApp today and its full potential is massive."

*Sources: Reuters, The Indian Eye, Inc42, Bar and Bench, Storyboard18*
